submit.title: Submit an event
submit.intro: This site updates via GitHub. There are two ways to submit an event:
submit.issueBody: Fastest for most people. Fill in our template with the name, date, location, and link — we'll add it to /data/events.
submit.issueMobileHint: Form not working, or looking odd on mobile?
submit.issueSimpleCta: Try the simple mobile-friendly version instead
submit.prBody: If you're already familiar with the structure: add a new JSON file to /data/events/ following the schema and open a PR. A GitHub Actions job validates the file automatically.
submit.prMobileTip: Tip: the PR flow works best on desktop. On mobile, try requesting "Desktop site" in your browser if the buttons don't respond.
submit.guidelines: Please make sure dates, timezone, and links are accurate — we double-check before publishing.

about.title: About
about.p1: Skateboard Event Calendar brings together skateboarding competitions from around the world in one place — from world championships and pro tours like SLS and X Games, to national cups and local jams.
about.p2: Every event is manually verified against a real source (the organizer's own site, an official calendar, or a news article) before being added — see the "Source" link at the bottom of each event page.
about.p3: The code is publicly viewable on GitHub for transparency, built by Martin Björck. Community submissions of new events are very welcome.

contact.title: Contact
contact.intro: Have a question, found an error, or want to suggest an event? Open an Issue on GitHub — it's the fastest way to reach us.
contact.issuesBody: Works for everything: incorrect event info, technical bugs, event suggestions, or general questions.
contact.responseTime: We usually respond within a few days. This is a community-run project without a dedicated support team.

disciplines.metaDescription: An in-depth guide to skateboarding's disciplines — Street, Park, Vert, Bowl, Freestyle and Slalom — including official 2026 World Skate competition rules.
disciplines.intro: Skateboarding isn't one single sport. It's several distinct disciplines with different terrain, techniques, rules, and competition formats. Here we cover the most important disciplines, including official definitions from World Skate (2026) where relevant.
disciplines.filterHint: Not sure what the disciplines mean?
disciplines.sourcesNote: Sources: World Skate Competition Rules – Slalom & Vert (Update August 2026) and established skate culture.
disciplines.ctaText: See upcoming events in this discipline

street.title: Street
street.body: Street is by far the most common discipline in modern skateboarding. Riders use the urban environment, or a purpose-built course imitating it: stairs, rails, curbs, gaps, ledges, and manuals.
features: Focus on technical flip tricks, grinds, slides, and manuals
Creativity and "line" thinking matter more than sheer amplitude
Usually individual runs (45–60 seconds) or best-trick format
street.formatNote: SLS (Street League) runs a knockout system with runs + best trick. Olympic Street includes both runs and best trick.
street.whyNote: It requires the least infrastructure and reflects how most people actually skate day to day.

park.title: Park
park.body: Park is skated in a designed skatepark with transitions, hips, bowls, spines, and quarterpipes. It's a hybrid between street and vert — speed, air, and technical tricks all blend together.
features: Higher speed and bigger air than street
Judged on difficulty, execution, use of course, flow, and consistency
park.eventsNote: Major events: X Games Park, World Skate Park World Championships, Olympic Park.

vert.title: Vert
vert.body: Vert (vertical) is skated on a large halfpipe, often 3.5–4 meters tall with a vertical wall. It's the classic "big air" discipline.
vert.qualifyingBody: Best of two (up to four) runs of 30–45 seconds. Five judges score 0.00–100. The highest and lowest scores are dropped, the middle three are averaged.
finalItems: 3 runs of 30 seconds each (best run counts)
Total score = best run + two best single tricks
criteria: Use of Vert ramp and features
vert.helmetNote: A helmet is mandatory for all ages in Vert under World Skate's 2026 rules.
vert.legends: Tony Hawk, Bucky Lasek, Andy Macdonald, Sandro Dias, Gui Khury.

bowl.title: Bowl / Pool
bowl.body: Bowl is the modern version of the old swimming pools the Z-Boys skated in the 1970s. Courses are deep, organic, and usually feature "pool coping".
features: Focus on lines, speed, lip tricks, and style
Less "tricks for points", more flow than modern Park
Usually open jams or invitational formats
bowl.eventsNote: Major events: Red Bull Bowl Rippers, Poolarama, Vans Pool Party (historically).

freestyle.title: Freestyle
freestyle.body: Freestyle is the oldest competitive discipline. Riders perform tricks on flat ground, often set to music, with an extreme focus on balance, spins, holds, and flatground technique.
freestyle.eventsNote: Major events: World Freestyle Skateboarding Championships.

slalom.title: Slalom
slalom.body: Slalom is a pure racing discipline where the rider passes cones in an alternating left/right pattern. Time is all that counts, with time penalties for knocked-down cones.
slalom.subTitle: The official sub-disciplines

hs.name: Hybrid / Special (HS/SS)
hs.character: Mix of short and medium turns

penalties: Tight / Straight / Hybrid: +0.1 sec per cone
slalom.dqNote: More than 9 knocked-down cones = disqualification (the Race Director may set a lower limit).
slalom.startNote: Starts are made from a ramp (at least 0.75 m tall) using either a random beep or a fixed countdown.

miniramp.title: Mini-ramp
miniramp.body: A smaller halfpipe (often 1.5–2.2 m). Popular with both pros and amateurs.

besttrick.title: Best Trick
besttrick.body: Only one trick counts. Common in street and park events.

downhill.title: Downhill / Speed
downhill.body: High-speed riding down a hill (often on a longboard).

history.pageTitle: Skateboarding History – From Surfers to an Olympic Sport
history.metaDescription: Skateboarding's history from 1950s California to the Olympic debut in Tokyo — the Z-Boys, urethane wheels, the vert golden age, the street era, and the Olympic era.
history.intro: Skateboarding is one of the few sports to go from a local Californian subculture to a global Olympic discipline in just over 70 years. Here is the deeper history.
history.sourcesNote: Sources: World Skate Competition Rules (Update August 2026) and established skateboarding history.
history.closingText: Skateboarding has kept its core — freedom, creativity, and community — despite going from the street to Olympic arenas.

era1950.title: 1950s–1960s: The Beginning
era1950.body: In the late 1950s, surfers in Southern California began bolting roller-skate wheels onto wooden planks to "surf" when the ocean was flat. The first commercial boards (Roller Derby, Makaha) appeared around 1959–1963. Wheels were made of metal or clay — grip was poor and speeds were low.

era1970.title: The 1970s: The Revolution
changes: Urethane wheels (Frank Nasworthy, 1972–73) — suddenly it was possible to go fast and actually control the board.

Dogtown & Z-Boys (Santa Monica/Venice) — a group of teenagers who started skating in emptied swimming pools during the drought. Tony Alva, Jay Adams, Stacy Peralta and others created a new, aggressive style.
Vert is born — halfpipes started being built and the first generation of vert skaters emerged.
era1970.outro: Skateboarding went from toy to youth culture. Skateboarder magazine and later Thrasher (1981) became central.

era1980.title: The 1980s: The Vert Golden Age
bullets: Freestyle was still huge (Rodney Mullen revolutionized flatground).
Tony Hawk, Christian Hosoi, Lance Mountain, Steve Caballero, and the Bones Brigade (Powell-Peralta) dominated.
Vision, Santa Cruz, and Powell were the big brands.
Vert contests were the main attraction at the major events.

era1990.title: The 1990s: Street Takes Over
bullets: Mark Gonzales, Mike Carroll, Eric Koston, Guy Mariano, Tom Penny, and the new generation defined the technical style.
Tech-deck tricks, handrails, and switch-stance skating became standard.
X Games launched in 1995, giving the sport massive TV exposure.
Companies like Girl, Chocolate, Emerica, Lakai, and Independent emerged.
The Berrics, 411VM, and Transworld became the new media platforms.

era2000.title: The 2000s–2010s: Professionalization
bullets: Street League Skateboarding (SLS) launched in 2010 under Rob Dyrdek's leadership, creating a clear pro tour with major prize money.
Female riders gained more visibility (Elissa Steamer, Cara-Beth Burnside, later Leticia Bufoni, Samarria Brevard, Sky Brown, Rayssa Leal).
Brazil, Japan, and Australia became new powerhouses.

era2020.title: The 2020s: The Olympic Era
bullets: Skateboarding debuted at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics (held in 2021) with Street and Park.
World Skate became the official international federation.
The sport became more global than ever — strong scenes in Brazil, Japan, Sweden, South Africa, China, and France.
X Games, SLS, the World Skate World Tour, and continental championships all run in parallel.
Vert has regained focus with official World Skate rules and rankings (WSVR).
